profiles.meeting_scenario: At a mid-sized academic medical center, the Associate Dean for Undergraduate Medical Education and the Director of Clinical Simulation are holding a brainstorming meeting to shape a new med-school pilot called 'Technology-Enhanced Diagnostics.' The pilot is meant to respond to recent interest in AI-assisted learning, simulation, and innovative devices by giving students early exposure to handheld ultrasound, smart airway tools, and AI-supported case review. The immediate context is that the dean has asked for a concept note within two weeks for possible inclusion in next spring's curriculum innovation funding cycle. The agenda is to generate feasible pilot formats, identify which technologies could anchor the experience, and sketch what would make the idea ready to circulate to faculty leads. The expected outcome is not a final design, but a shared-looking set of candidate ideas that each participant believes can be turned into a pilot proposal quickly.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Associate Dean for Undergraduate Medical Education
members.expertise: Curriculum design, clerkship integration, educational assessment
members.background: An internist who moved into medical education leadership after running the third-year curriculum reform process; she regularly works with course directors, accreditation teams, and the dean's office.
members.private_state: She wants a concept that sounds innovative but can be inserted into the curriculum with minimal disruption, produces a persuasive early story for the dean, and does not require negotiating a large new staffing commitment before funding is secured.
hidden_assumptions: When curriculum leaders say 'simulation,' it includes screen-based cases, device demos, and low-risk practice formats, not only sim-center sessions.
A 'pilot' is successful if it is credible enough to socialize with clerkship directors and generate expansion interest, even if delivery still relies on central support.
The 'new ultrasound devices' available to education discussions are the handheld units purchased through the school's innovation grant, regardless of which department currently stores them.
To show early impact, short LMS reflections and student confidence surveys are sufficient for an initial concept note.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.role: Director of Clinical Simulation and Digital Learning
members.expertise: Simulation operations, device-based teaching, faculty facilitator training, learning technologies
members.background: A biomedical engineer by training who now runs the simulation center, oversees procedural trainers and device inventory, and supports multiple residency and undergraduate programs with operational rollout.
members.private_state: He wants any idea that emerges to be operationally coherent, tied to equipment his team can actually schedule and maintain, and structured in a way that does not create vague commitments the sim center will later be expected to absorb without preparation.
hidden_assumptions: At this institution, 'simulation' normally means facilitated activity delivered through the sim center, using rooms, equipment, workflows, and staff oversight.
The 'new ultrasound devices' relevant for teaching plans are the cart-based units recently transferred into sim inventory, because those are the devices his team can reliably schedule and support.
Something is not truly 'faculty-ready' unless facilitators can independently run the session after formal prep, without depending on ad hoc central troubleshooting.
Documenting early impact should rely on observable performance data, simulator logs, and facilitator checklists rather than mainly self-reported learner impressions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk positively about making the pilot 'simulation-based.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a broad simulation umbrella that can include tablet-based clinical cases, guided device demonstrations, and one brief in-person practice component outside a full sim-center workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means structured sim-center sessions with dedicated rooms, facilitated debriefing, and hands-on stations using managed equipment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In medical education, 'simulation' is a respected, familiar umbrella term, so each hears the other as reinforcing the same idea rather than signaling a different delivery model.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'new ultrasound devices' they are referring to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both suggest anchoring the experience around 'the new ultrasound devices.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the six handheld POCUS units bought through the campus innovation grant and used intermittently in preclinical anatomy teaching.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the two cart-based SonoSite units recently reassigned from anesthesia to the simulation center.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know the school has recently acquired ultrasound equipment, and the phrase sounds specific enough to imply shared reference even though there are multiple plausible 'new' devices in circulation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree it would be ideal to have something 'faculty-ready by January.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means having a polished concept note, sample materials, and enough structure that clerkship leaders can review and tentatively adopt the idea for spring.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means trained facilitators, tested logistics, equipment scheduling, and a deliverable session that faculty can independently run in January.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like ordinary project shorthand, and both assume the other is using the institution's common sense meaning of readiness without needing to unpack operational versus proposal readiness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot should generate 'early impact data' for the dean.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means short post-session LMS surveys, learner reflections, and quick confidence ratings that can be summarized in a concept memo.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means station completion records, faculty observation checklists, and performance traces pulled from sim platforms and device use logs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they agree that some evidence is needed and neither is yet choosing a formal study design, each treats 'impact data' as a settled practical detail rather than something requiring clarification.

turns.inner_thought: The dean wants something that reads as forward-looking without opening a giant implementation negotiation before we've even secured funding. If I can frame this as technology-enhanced diagnostics with a credible pilot shape, I can get clerkship directors interested. It does not need to be fully built out yet; it needs to sound coherent, timely, and easy to socialize.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The dean asked for a set of brainstormed ideas for a spring pilot on Technology-Enhanced Diagnostics—something that shows how innovations and devices are changing medical education. We only need a strong concept note in the near term, but it should feel concrete enough that faculty leads can see where it might fit.

turns.inner_thought: If this is going to land anywhere real, it should be built around a format my team can actually support. Simulation-based gives it structure and legitimacy, and the two new cart-based ultrasound units in sim inventory are scheduleable. If we pair those with one additional smart device, I can envision a workable station model instead of a vague innovation showcase that later falls on us to operationalize.
turns.utterance: My first reaction is that the strongest angle may be to make it simulation-based and anchor it around the new ultrasound devices, plus one other smart device students could rotate through. That gives it a clear spine and keeps the technology tied to actual diagnostic decision-making.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—that lets us package this broadly. By simulation-based, I'm thinking students could do tablet cases and AI-supported review before clerkships, then have a brief hands-on experience with the handheld units and maybe one device demo. That keeps contact time light and avoids needing a heavy sim-center footprint while still sounding substantive.
turns.utterance: I like that. We could think of it as a simulation package that students partly complete on tablets before clerkships, followed by a short in-person hands-on component. That would let us introduce the technology in a way that feels connected rather than isolated.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's aligned on a structured flow. I can picture reserving several sim bays, moving learners in small groups between the two ultrasound carts, an airway device station, and a debrief area. Pre-work is fine if it supports the session, but the core has to be a facilitated sim-center experience or it won't hold together operationally.
turns.utterance: Yes, and from a flow standpoint I can imagine reserving a few bays and splitting learners between the new ultrasound devices, an airway station, and a debrief point so they rotate cleanly. That would make the experience feel intentional rather than like a collection of unrelated demos.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this explicitly light-touch. This is a pilot, not a full curricular launch. If by January I have a polished concept note, sample materials, and enough structure to put in front of the medicine clerkship director, that's a win. I do not want to imply we need a fully staffed rollout before the dean even sees it.
turns.utterance: The main thing from my side is that it should stay light because this is just a pilot. If we can get something faculty-ready by January, I could start socializing it with a medicine clerkship block first and see where there’s appetite.

turns.inner_thought: January is reasonable only if readiness means actual delivery readiness. We'd need a December train-the-trainer, facilitator checkoff, room logic, equipment scheduling, and a session faculty can run without my staff rescuing it ad hoc. I need to steer this toward a contained operational commitment now, before assumptions drift.
turns.utterance: I think January is feasible, especially if we use December for a train-the-trainer approach so faculty are checked off and can run the sessions themselves once we launch. That would make the handoff much cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: The dean will absolutely ask what evidence we have, but for an early concept memo I don't need a full outcomes study. Short LMS reflections and confidence ratings are enough to show students found value and that the model deserves expansion discussion. Keep it simple, quick, and presentable.
turns.utterance: And we should build in a simple way to generate early impact data for the dean. I’d want to know what students felt they learned and whether the format seems worth expanding.

turns.inner_thought: That's straightforward if we capture actual activity. We can use simulator records, facilitator observation sheets, and maybe platform traces if there's a digital component. Self-report alone won't be enough for me to call it useful evidence, but she's probably just signaling that data should be easy to summarize.
turns.utterance: That should be manageable. We can pull together early impact data from usage information and facilitator observation sheets so we can show how learners moved through the stations and where they seemed to gain traction.

turns.inner_thought: This is sounding exactly like something I can sell upstairs: a simulation-based pilot, centered on the handheld ultrasound units and a few other technologies, with materials polished enough by January to circulate and some early survey-style data for the concept note. I don't need every logistical detail today; I just need a clean summary line.
turns.utterance: So, if I’m hearing it right, we’re talking about a simulation-based pilot built around the new ultrasound devices, ideally faculty-ready by January, with early impact data we can include in the concept note. That feels like the right level of specificity for now.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll turn this into something operationally coherent: equipment, bays, facilitators, sequence, and training assumptions. She can craft the proposal narrative while I make sure it doesn't become an amorphous promise the sim center is expected to absorb later. If we reconvene next week, I should have a draft plan grounded in resources I can actually schedule.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. I’ll sketch the equipment and facilitation plan, and you can draft the proposal language, then we can reconvene next week with a more concrete pilot outline.
